content.text: Sometimes a single IF/ELSE is not enough to express the full logic of a problem. When a program needs to check a second condition ONLY IF a first condition is true — or only if it is false — nested conditionals are the solution. Nested conditionals place IF statements inside other IF statements, creating a tree of decisions.

content.definition: Conditional statements within conditional statements. Allow programs to check multiple conditions in sequence, where inner conditions are only evaluated if outer conditions are met.

content.text: The defining characteristic of nested conditionals is dependency: the inner conditional is only reached and evaluated IF the outer conditional's path leads there. If the outer condition sends execution to the ELSE branch, the inner conditional inside the IF branch is completely skipped — never evaluated at all.

rows: Inner never reached when outer is false

content.label: Key Idea
content.text: The inner conditional is ONLY evaluated when execution reaches it — which only happens when the outer condition directs execution to that branch. If the outer IF is false and execution goes to the outer ELSE, any inner conditionals inside the outer IF block are completely ignored.

One of the most common uses of nested conditionals is classifying a value into multiple non-overlapping categories. A grading system with letter grades is a perfect example — each grade boundary is only checked if higher boundaries have already been ruled out.

Notice that each inner condition is only evaluated when all outer conditions have been false. For score = 85, we check ≥ 90 (false), then check ≥ 80 (true) and stop. We never check ≥ 70 because execution has already found its branch and exited the nested structure.

Sometimes a nested conditional can be rewritten as a single IF with an AND expression. Other times, the nested version is necessary because the two cases need different actions. Understanding when to use each is important.

rows: IF(x > 0) { IF(x < 10) { DISPLAY "in range" } ELSE { DISPLAY "too big" } } ELSE { DISPLAY "too small" }
When each combination of true/false needs a different action — 3 or more distinct outcomes
When you only need one action if both conditions are true — simpler and more readable for 2 outcomes

content.text: When tracing nested conditionals on the exam, always work from the OUTSIDE in. Evaluate the outermost condition first. Based on true or false, determine which branch you are in. Then — and only then — evaluate the next condition inside that branch. Continue inward step by step.

content.label: Exam Tip
content.text: When tracing nested conditionals: work OUTSIDE-IN. Evaluate the outermost condition first. If it is true, enter the outer IF — now evaluate the inner conditions inside that block. If it is false, enter the outer ELSE — evaluate the inner conditions inside that block. Never evaluate an inner condition in a branch you have not entered.
Summary: What to Know for the Exam

items: Nested conditional statements are conditional statements within conditional statements
Inner conditions are ONLY evaluated if the outer condition directs execution to that branch
If the outer IF is false and execution goes to the ELSE, any inner conditionals inside the outer IF block are never evaluated
Always trace nested conditionals from the OUTSIDE IN — evaluate the outermost condition first
A common use is multi-level classification where each condition is only checked after higher-priority conditions have been ruled out
A nested conditional with one action for combined true/true can sometimes be simplified to a single IF with AND — use nested when different combinations need different actions
The ELSE belongs to the nearest IF above it at the same nesting level — be careful to track which ELSE pairs with which IF
